findings.summary: The `bounds=(0.5, 2.0)` passed to minimize_scalar is not a 'sane bounded search range' for the brief's own stated scenarios — verified numerically by scanning NLL(T) over a wide range for the exact synthetic fixtures used in the new tests. For the overconfident fixture (200 samples, single-class logit=10.0, 50% argmax accuracy), NLL is still monotonically decreasing at T=2.0 (NLL≈2.59) and only bottoms out around T≈15-20 (NLL≈1.05) — more than 2x lower NLL than what the bound allows. For the 'well-calibrated' fixture (deterministic always-correct predictions, logit=2.0), the model is actually underconfident at T=1 (confidence 78.7% vs 100% accuracy), so the true unconstrained minimizer heads toward T→0, and the bounded fit just pins to the lower boundary (measured T≈0.5003). In both cases fit_temperature silently returns a boundary-clamped value with no indication it isn't the actual minimizer — for any real held-out set requiring T outside [0.5, 2.0] (well documented in calibration literature, e.g. Guo et al. 2017), this function will silently under- or over-correct.

findings.summary: test_fit_temperature_on_perfectly_calibrated_returns_near_1 asserts `0.5 < T < 3.0`, but the actual fitted value (verified by running the fit) is T≈0.5003 — pinned at the lower search bound, not 'near 1.0' as the test name and brief claim. This isn't a coincidence of a slightly-off assertion: the fixture itself (deterministic, always-correct predictions) is not actually well-calibrated at T=1 (accuracy 100% vs confidence 78.7%), so its true NLL-minimizing T heads toward 0, and the test only passes because minimize_scalar's lower bound (line 25 in calibration.py) happens to land inside the asserted range. The companion test at line 46 (`assert T > 1.5`) has the same issue in the other direction — the fitted T≈2.0 is the upper search bound, not a genuine converged minimizer (true unconstrained minimum is ≈15-20). Neither test would catch a fit_temperature that always returns the nearest bound regardless of the data.
